A.explanation: R cannot get brighter because total resistance rises when Q breaks, so the current through R falls and $P = I^2R$ for R falls.

B.explanation: P takes a larger share of the battery e.m.f. so its power $P = V^2/R$ rises, while the smaller total current makes R dissipate less power.

C.explanation: P cannot get dimmer because the voltage across the P-Q parallel block increases when the current through series lamp R decreases.

D.explanation: P gets brighter, not dimmer, because removal of the parallel branch Q forces more voltage across the remaining lamp P.

hints: Notice that P and Q are in parallel with each other, and that parallel block is in series with R.
Think how the resistance of the P-Q block changes from $R/2$ to $R$ when Q becomes an open circuit, and what this does to total current through R.
Compare the voltage across R before and after using $V = IR$, then use the fixed battery e.m.f. to decide what happens to the voltage left across P.
walkthrough: Identify the circuit: lamps P and Q are in parallel, and lamp R is in series with that combination across a battery of negligible internal resistance.
Recall brightness follows power: $P = I^2R$ for a series lamp and $P = V^2/R$ for a lamp with voltage across it, with identical lamp resistance $R$.
When Q breaks, the parallel resistance rises from $R/2$ to $R$, so total circuit resistance rises and total current $I = E/R_{total}$ falls.
Lamp R carries this total current, so its power $I^2R$ falls and R gets dimmer.
The voltage across R, $V_R = IR$, falls, so the voltage left for the parallel block, $V_P = E - V_R$, must rise.
Lamp P now has larger $V_P$ across the same resistance, so $V_P^2/R$ rises and P gets brighter. This is option B.
